Context/Background:
Intraductal papillary neoplasms (IPNs),  including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasms (IOPNs), and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasms (ITPNs), are clinically detectable macroscopic non-invasive cyst-forming lesions, some of which progress to invasive pancreatic cancer. Proteins and glycoproteins have proven to be useful clinical biomarkers for classifying cyst-forming neoplasms in the pancreas.Here, we used proteomics and glycoproteomics to characterize a series of histologically and genetically well-characterized surgically resected IPNs, including IPMNs and IOPNs.

Our analysis included 69 IPNs (64 IPMNs and 5 IOPNs), 76 macro-dissected grossly normal duct tissues (NDs, with 32 of the 76 NDs coming from the same resection specimens as the IPNs), and 32 cyst fluid samples (22 from matched IPMN patients, 3 matched IOPN patients, 2 from unrelated IPMN patients, and 5 other cysts).
Prompt: Look at the differential genes between high and low grade IPMN and between high grade IPMN and ND. From the commonly upregulated proteins, nominate a few important genes that are related to Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in the literature.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
This analysis examines differential protein expression in surgically resected intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) of the pancreas, comparing high-grade (HG) versus low-grade (LG) IPMNs and HG IPMN versus matched normal duct tissue (ND) using proteomics (Table S2M, Wang et al. 2025). Key details not specified in the input: patient age/sex distribution, MS experimental platform, precise sample numbers per contrast beyond summary counts. The primary signals are a set of 279 proteins significantly upregulated in both HG vs LG IPMN and HG IPMN vs ND (FDR < 0.05, fold-change > 0).  

Keywords  
• IPMN progression  • Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)  • Cell-cycle/DNA replication  • Proteolysis  • Endocytosis  

Candidate Genes  
Based on overlap in both contrasts and literature relevance to PDAC, we prioritize:  
TFRC, SPINT2, LGALS9, HMGB3, MCM3, MCM7, ACOT7  

Pathway Enrichments  
GSEA was run on the 279 common upregulated genes using GSEA preranked (corr_col=“HG IPMN vs ND”). Ratios of up/down enriched terms per library (up vs down vs total):  
KEGG_2016: 23 / 18 / 41 (56 % up, 44 % down, ratio 1.28)  
GO_Biological_Process_2023: 136 / 73 / 209 (65 % up, 35 % down, ratio 1.86)  
Reactome_Pathways_2024: 93 / 71 / 164 (57 % up, 43 % down, ratio 1.31)  
MSigDB_Hallmark_2020: 8 / 1 / 9 (89 % up, 11 % down, ratio 8.0)  

KEGG_2016 (UP)  
| Theme            | Direction | Leading Genes (selected)                       |  
|------------------|-----------|------------------------------------------------|  
| Endocytosis      | UP        | TGFB2, MET, LDLR, RAB35, TFRC, CLTC,…          |  
| Phagosome        | UP        | ITGAV, FCGR3A, HLA-A, HLA-B, TFRC, CTSL,…      |  
| Epstein-Barr virus infection | UP | HDAC1, RB1, STAT3, MAPK10, IRAK1, POLR2H… |  

KEGG_2016 (DOWN)  
| Theme                          | Direction | Leading Genes                      |  
|--------------------------------|-----------|------------------------------------|  
| Pancreatic secretion           | DOWN      | AMY2A, CELA3A, PRSS1, CPA1, CPA2… |  
| Protein digestion and absorption | DOWN    | COL4A2, CEL, PRSS2, CELA2A, CPA1… |  

GO_Biological_Process_2023 (UP)  
| Theme                  | Direction | Leading Genes (selected)      |  
|------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------|  
| Membrane Organization  | UP        | STAM2, SYNGR2, VAMP3, EXOC7,… |  
| Endosomal Transport    | UP        | RAB35, SNX1, CLTC, PICALM,…   |  

GO_Biological_Process_2023 (DOWN)  
| Theme              | Direction | Leading Genes            |  
|--------------------|-----------|--------------------------|  
| Proteolysis        | DOWN      | PRSS1, CELA3A, CTRB2,…  |  
| Cytoplasmic Translation | DOWN | RPL22, RPS9, EIF4A2,…    |  

Reactome_Pathways_2024 (UP)  
| Theme                  | Direction | Leading Genes (selected)       |  
|------------------------|-----------|--------------------------------|  
| RHO GTPase Effectors   | UP        | ACTB, TUBB4A, WAS, MYH9,…      |  

Reactome_Pathways_2024 (DOWN)  
| Theme                                   | Direction | Leading Genes                   |  
|-----------------------------------------|-----------|---------------------------------|  
| Metabolism of Amino Acids and Derivatives | DOWN    | RPL22, RPS9, CHDH, SRM,…        |  
| SRP-dependent Cotranslational Protein Targeting | DOWN | SRP68, SEC61B, RPL34,…  |  

MSigDB_Hallmark_2020 (UP)  
| Theme                    | Direction | Leading Genes (selected)            |  
|--------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------|  
| Interferon Gamma Response| UP        | IRF8, TAP1, STAT1, CD38,…           |  
| E2F Targets              | UP        | MCM3, MCM5, MCM7, POLD1,…           |  

MSigDB_Hallmark_2020 (DOWN)  
| Theme               | Direction | Leading Genes                 |  
|---------------------|-----------|-------------------------------|  
| KRAS Signaling Dn   | DOWN      | CLPS, CPA2, CPB1, HNF1A,…    |  

Analysis  
GSEA reveals strong upregulation of vesicular trafficking–based pathways (Endocytosis, Phagosome, membrane/endosomal organization) and cell-cycle/DNA-replication modules (E2F Targets, MCMs), consistent with proliferative reprogramming during IPMN progression. Simultaneously, acinar/digestive functions (Pancreatic secretion, Proteolysis) are repressed, mirroring loss of differentiated exocrine phenotype. GO and Reactome underscore this dual biology: enhanced membrane remodeling and DNA replication at the expense of proteolytic and translational machinery. The Hallmark KRAS Signaling_Dn downregulation echoes the known KRAS-driven dedifferentiation axis in PDAC, while IFN-γ response up suggests emerging immune–tumor interactions in high-grade lesions.  

Targeted (keyword-guided) subset  
Filtering GSEA results for “cell cycle,” “replication,” and candidate genes (MCM3, MCM7, TFRC) highlights:  
• KEGG DNA replication (UP; NES 3.15; Lead: MCM3, MCM5, MCM6, MCM7, POLD1)  
• Hallmark E2F Targets (UP; NES 3.16; Lead: MCM3, MCM7, MCM5, TFRC)  
These terms were absent from top ORA lists without filtering and emerged only when focusing on MCM family and TFRC.  

Key Genes/Proteins (leading edge)  
Upregulated  
| Gene  | Direction | Role/Function              | Pathway(s)                 |  
|-------|-----------|----------------------------|----------------------------|  
| MCM3  | UP        | DNA replication licensing  | DNA replication, E2F Targets |  
| MCM7  | UP        | DNA helicase component     | DNA replication, E2F Targets |  
| TFRC  | UP        | Iron uptake receptor       | Endocytosis, E2F Targets    |  

Downregulated  
(Note: no shared core genes among strongly downregulated hallmark terms with direct PDAC literature links)  

Comparisons  
MCM3/7 and TFRC show concordant upregulation across contrasts (IPMN HG vs LG and HG vs ND). No discordant single-contrast findings among these key genes.  

Implications  
MCM3/7 overexpression is widely reported in PDAC as a marker of proliferation and poor prognosis. TFRC upregulation facilitates iron import to sustain redox balance in rapidly dividing pancreatic lesions. SPINT2 and HMGB3 (not shown in detailed tables) are also implicated in PDAC invasiveness and stemness. Therapeutically, targeting DNA replication licensing (e.g., MCM inhibitors) or iron metabolism (anti-TFRC antibodies) may restrain IPMN progression to invasive PDAC.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate MCM3/7 and TFRC protein expression by IHC across IPMN grades and correlate with patient outcome.  
2. Assess functional dependency using PDAC cell models (e.g., TFRC knockdown or MCM complex inhibitors) to confirm vulnerability.  
3. Clarify whether IFN-γ pathway activation reflects immune infiltration or tumor-intrinsic signaling.  
4. Check presence/absence of KRAS Signaling upregulation in IPMN cyst fluid proteome (for non-tissue biomarkers).  

References  
None (no PMIDs directly obtained via Steps 5–6)
